events.title: St. Oswald falls at Maserfield
events.shortBlurb: The king who had brought Aidan and the monks of Iona to Northumbria was slain by the pagan Penda of Mercia, and numbered at once among the martyrs…
body: Oswald, son of King Æthelfrith of Bernicia, had spent his youth in exile among the Irish monks of Iona and there been baptized. Returning, he overthrew the British king Cadwallon at the Heavenfield near the Roman Wall, in 634 by the common reckoning, setting up with his own hands a wooden cross before the battle; and he sent to Iona for a bishop. In 635 Aidan came, and Oswald gave him the island of Lindisfarne for his see, translating the Irishman's preaching for his thegns until the English speech came to him.

For eight years he ruled Northumbria, the strongest of the English kings, whom Bede numbers among those who held the lordship of the southern nations. On 5 August, in 642 as the chronicle reckons, he met Penda, the pagan king of the Mercians, in battle at the place called Maserfield — Oswestry, Oswald's Tree, as the English came to name it — and was slain there, dying, Bede tells, with a prayer for the souls of his soldiers, which passed into a proverb.

Penda set his head and arms upon stakes. His brother Oswiu recovered them: the head was laid at Lindisfarne, the arms at Bamburgh, where his right hand, Bede records, remained uncorrupted. Miracles were told of the very soil where he fell, and the dead king was venerated as a martyr from that day.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 August
